Requirements:
1. Determine the 10 largest US publicly traded companies by CURRENT market cap (live, not from memory). Pull market caps from pricelib for a generous candidate list of ~30 mega caps (NWB, NWC, NWI, NWD, NWD2, NWE, NWF, NWH, NWG, NWJ, NWK, NWL, NWO, V, ORCL, MA, NWM, NFLX, COST, UNH, JNJ, PLTR, AMD, HD, PG, BAC, ABBV, etc.) and rank. Count Alphabet once (use NWD, combine both share classes' market cap for ranking if pricelib reports them separately; use whatever pricelib reports for the company). 2. Daily adjusted close (auto_adjust=True, i.e. total-return-adjusted) for those 10 over the trailing 12 months: 2025-10-21 through 2026-10-21.
3. Benchmarks over the same window: Index 500 cap-weighted = ^GSPC, Index 500 equal-weighted = ^SPXEW. If ^SPXEW is unavailable or patchy on pricelib, fall back to NWRSP (Invesco Index 500 Equal Weight ETF) and note it. Also include NWSPY and NWRSP as total-return ETF proxies alongside the indices (indices are price-only).
4. Workbook sheets, exact names and layout (another script depends on this):
   - "Prices": column A "Date" (dates, ascending), then one column per ticker; the 10 stocks first in market-cap order, then benchmarks. Column headers = ticker symbols exactly. Align on common trading dates; don't forward-fill across more than isolated gaps.
   - "Returns": same layout, daily simple returns (first row dropped).
   - "Info": one row per ticker: Ticker, Name, Type (Stock/Benchmark), Market Cap (USD, stocks only), Rank, Notes. Plus a row or footer stating data source (Pricefeed Finance via pricelib), pull date, window.
   Format: freeze header row, sensible number formats, date column formatted as date, reasonable column widths.
5. Sanity check: no all-NaN columns, ~250 rows, last date is the most recent trading day, spot-check one price is plausible.

Report back briefly: the 10 tickers with market caps in order, which EW benchmark ticker was used, row count/date range, any data issues. Do not dump data.

Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.

Write a Python script at /Users/user/Desktop/proj-run-15/claude/portfolio_analysis.py that computes correlation tables and mean-variance optimization (MVO) plots from an Excel workbook of prices.

Environment: venv at /Users/user/Desktop/proj-run-15/claude/.venv with pandas, numpy, scipy, matplotlib, openpyxl installed. Use `.venv/bin/python`. Don't add other dependencies.

Input contract (workbook is being produced in parallel by another agent at /Users/user/Desktop/proj-run-15/claude/market_data.xlsx; it may not exist yet):
- Sheet "Prices": column "Date" then one column per ticker (daily adjusted close).
- Sheet "Info": columns Ticker, Name, Type ("Stock" or "Benchmark"), Market Cap, Rank, Notes (may contain extra footer rows - be robust: only use rows where Type is Stock/Benchmark).
- Benchmarks are tickers like ^GSPC, ^SPXEW, NWSPY, NWRSP.

Script behavior (argparse CLI, sensible defaults so `python portfolio_analysis.py` just works):
- --input (default market_data.xlsx next to script), --output-dir (default ./output), --rf annual risk-free rate (default 0.04), --freq daily|weekly|monthly returns (default daily; resample prices then pct_change), --allow-short flag (default long-only), --max-weight optional per-asset cap, --tickers optional subset, --n-random number of random portfolios for the cloud (default 5000), --seed.
- Optimization universe = Stock tickers (from Info Type; if Info missing, treat tickers starting with ^ or in {NWSPY,NWRSP} as benchmarks). Benchmarks are NOT optimized over but are plotted as reference points and included in correlation tables.
- Annualize with 252/52/12 periods.
- Correlation: full Pearson correlation matrix (stocks + benchmarks) -> correlation heatmap PNG (annotated values, diverging colormap centered at 0, clean labels) and written to an output Excel file. Also include annualized covariance matrix and a summary stats table (ann. return, ann. vol, Sharpe, max drawdown, beta vs ^GSPC if present) in that output workbook.
- MVO with scipy.optimize (SLSQP): efficient frontier (trace ~50-100 target returns between min-variance and max achievable return), global min-variance portfolio, max-Sharpe (tangency) portfolio, and capital market line from rf through tangency. Respect long-only/short/max-weight constraints.
- MVO plot PNG: random portfolio cloud colored by Sharpe (with colorbar), frontier line, CML, markers for min-var and max-Sharpe, each individual stock labeled, benchmarks as distinct markers labeled. x = annualized vol, y = annualized return, percent axes. Second PNG: weights bar chart (or side-by-side) for min-var and max-Sharpe portfolios.
- Write weights + portfolio stats (return, vol, Sharpe) for min-var and max-Sharpe and frontier points into the output Excel file (separate sheets).
- Print a short console summary.
- Clean, readable, modular code (functions for load, returns, stats, optimize, plot, export), docstrings brief. Use matplotlib Agg backend. Plots should look professional: readable fonts, tight layout, dpi 150, title includes date range and frequency.

Testing: if market_data.xlsx doesn't exist yet, test with a synthetic workbook you generate in the workdir (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-user-Desktop-proj-run-15-claude/edf994a4-fa71-4c29-8c1b-bf6d73b1f312/workdir), matching the contract above (10 stocks + ^GSPC, ^SPXEW, NWSPY, NWRSP). Verify: weights sum to 1, long-only weights >= 0, max-Sharpe Sharpe >= every random portfolio Sharpe (within tolerance), min-var vol <= every frontier vol. Then, if the real market_data.xlsx exists by the time you're done, run against it too. Look at the output PNGs (Read tool can view images) to confirm they render well.

Report back briefly: CLI usage, outputs produced, test results, any caveats. Don't paste the code.

Build a short PowerPoint deck at /Users/user/Desktop/proj-run-15/claude/mega_cap_mvo.pptx. FIRST load the skill `anthropic-skills:pptx` via the Skill tool and follow its workflow (including rendering slides to images and visually checking them).

Inputs (project dir /Users/user/Desktop/proj-run-15/claude):
- output/correlation_heatmap.png, output/mvo_frontier.png, output/mvo_weights.png (final charts; don't regenerate)
- output/portfolio_analysis.xlsx (sheets incl. Summary Stats, Portfolio Stats, Weights) and market_data.xlsx (Info sheet: tickers, names, market caps)
- Python venv at .venv if you need it (pip install python-pptx into it if required).

Design: 16:9. Match the charts' palette exactly so the deck feels like one system: background #FBF8F2 (warm cream), text #22223B (ink), accents #0F7C80 (teal) and #E8505B (coral). Clean, minimal, generous whitespace, one sans-serif font. Charts are the hero on chart slides: large, not dissamd (preserve aspect ratio), commentary as 2-3 short lines beside or below. No clip art, no gradient junk. Small footer on content slides: "Source: Pricefeed Finance via pricelib. Daily returns 2025-10-22 to 2026-10-20. rf = 4%."

Slides and commentary (keep commentary light, use this wording, trimmed if needed; verify every number against the xlsx files and fix any that don't match):

1. Title: "Mega-Cap Correlation & Mean-Variance Analysis". Subtitle: "10 largest US companies vs. Index 500 (cap- and equal-weighted) · trailing 12 months · October 2026".

2. "The universe": compact table of the 10 stocks (ticker, name, market cap in $T, 1 decimal) plus the two benchmarks (^GSPC = Index 500, ^SPXEW = Index 500 Equal Weight). Add per-row annualized return and volatility from Summary Stats. One line: "Ten names worth ~$28T combined; ranked by live market cap on 21 Oct 2026." (compute the actual combined total and use it).

3. "Correlations are lower than the concentration story suggests" + heatmap. Commentary:
   - Most mega-cap pairs sit between 0.1 and 0.4. The clusters: NWI–NWH (0.53) and NWD–NWE (0.55).
   - NWJ and NWK are the diversifiers, near zero or negative against the tech names.
   - The cap-weighted index tracks the mega caps far more tightly than equal-weight (NWI: 0.65 vs 0.23). That's concentration showing up in the benchmark.

4. "The efficient frontier" + frontier chart. Commentary:
   - Min volatility: 11.0% vol, 17.1% return, Sharpe 1.19.
   - Max Sharpe: 16.3% vol, 34.6% return, Sharpe 1.87.
   - Add one line comparing to the benchmarks using ^GSPC and ^SPXEW return/vol/Sharpe from Summary Stats (e.g. "Both beat the Index 500's X% return at Y% vol over the period.") Only state what the numbers support.

5. "What the optimizer wants" + weights chart. Commentary:
   - Min vol is mostly NWJ (~60%), its low vol and low correlation do the work.
   - Max Sharpe spreads across NWK, NWB, NWD, NWJ and NWI, and zeros out NWC, NWE, NWF, NWH and NWG.

6. "Read with caution": 3 short lines:
   - One year of data, optimized in-sample: these weights describe the past year, not a forecast.
   - Expected returns are trailing realized returns, the noisiest MVO input; small changes swing the weights.
   - Index levels are price-only; stock prices are dividend-adjusted.

Use the en dash / plain hyphen in pairs like NWI–NWH fine; avoid em-dashes in commentary text.

Render to images, inspect every slide, fix overflow/overlap/misalignment. Report back in 3-4 lines: path, slide count, anything you changed from the given commentary and why. Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.

fields.message:
Restyle portfolio_analysis.py charts to a new, more professional design system. The current cream/coral look is being retired. Replace the palette block entirely:

  PAPER  #FFFFFF  (figure + axes background, pure white)
  INK    #18212F  (text, frontier line, axes)
  COBALT #1F3A93  (negative end of correlation scale, min volatility)
  AMBER  #C8890A  (positive end of correlation scale, max Sharpe; the one accent, use it nowhere else)
  MIST   #EEF0EC  (diverging midpoint)
  RULE   #C9CDD3  (grid lines, spines, secondary text)

Font: Franklin Gothic (Book for text, Demi for emphasis). On this machine the TTFs are in "/Applications/Microsoft PowerPoint.app/Contents/Resources/DFonts/" (Franklin Gothic Book.ttf, Franklin Gothic Demi.ttf, etc). Register them with matplotlib.font_manager.addfont at startup; if the files aren't present, fall back silently to the matplotlib default so the script stays portable.

Charts:
- Heatmap: diverging COBALT -> MIST -> AMBER, vmin -1 vmax 1. Lower triangle as now. Annotation text INK, switching to white only on dark cells (luminance check). Thin white cell gaps (linewidths ~1.5, white). Slim colorbar, no outline, RULE ticks.
- Frontier: cloud is a sequential single-hue cobalt ramp from a pale cobalt tint (~#C9D2EA) to COBALT, colored by Sharpe, alpha ~0.45, small dots. Frontier line INK, ~2pt. Min-vol marker COBALT, max-Sharpe marker AMBER (white edge). Labels: plain text in INK next to the markers (no boxed callouts; a thin RULE leader line is fine), two lines each: name, then "Sharpe 1.87 · 16.3% vol · 34.6% return" style is NOT wanted, use "Sharpe 1.87, vol 16.3%, return 34.6%". Slim colorbar "Sharpe ratio".
- Weights: horizontal bars, shared x-axis (keep), min-vol COBALT, max-Sharpe AMBER, value labels in INK only for weights >= 0.5%, zero weights show no label. Sort tickers in the same market-cap order as now.
- All: only left and bottom spines, in RULE; grid y-only (or x-only for bar charts) in very light RULE at low alpha; tick labels RULE-darkened (#5A6270 is fine as secondary text); sentence-case axis labels.

Add a `--no-titles` flag: when set, charts omit the figure title/subtitle entirely (the deck carries the message in slide titles). Without the flag, keep a single-line title in sentence case with the date range in smaller secondary text. Also add `--figsize W H` (inches, default 10 6) used for frontier and weights; heatmap stays near-square at default but respects --figsize if given. DPI 200.

Then generate TWO sets: default titled set into ./output, and a deck set with `--no-titles --figsize 8.6 5.4 --output-dir output/deck` (heatmap at the same 8.6 x 5.4 box: fit the triangle in it with a smaller font, it must be legible at slide size). Read every PNG and fix anything off. A deck builder is waiting on output/deck/*.png. Report in 2-3 lines. Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
